subtype: Approach: win the argument with facts and links [Pitfall]
passage:
Dear Deepak Mama,

I want to tell you what I did, because I keep going over it. For a week after the dinner I sent you articles: eleven links, three charts, and one table I made myself. I wrote 'see, here are the figures' under each one. I honestly thought that once you saw the evidence, you would have to agree.

Every link came back with a longer message from you, and a sharper one. On Sunday you left the table before the sweets were served. Mummy told me she felt caught between us.

I wanted to be right more than I wanted to hear you. I'm sorry it turned into a contest. I would like to start again with a cup of tea.

Parul

qa.q: How many links did Parul send Deepak Mama?
qa.a: Eleven links, plus three charts and one table.

qa.q: Why did Parul send so many articles?
qa.a: Parul wanted to win, believing that evidence alone would force agreement, so the sending grew out of a wish to be right.

qa.q: What could Parul do instead of forwarding more evidence, and why?
qa.a: Parul could ask Deepak Mama about his worries and listen before offering any facts, because facts are heard better once a person feels understood.

qa.q: How does Deepak Mama's Sunday exit show what the articles did to him?
qa.a: Leaving before the sweets suggests he felt attacked and defensive rather than persuaded, so each fact made the debate a contest of who was right.

grounding: The student forwards statistics and articles to prove the uncle wrong, and each fact hardens resistance.
